In 1991, [WiLAN](/wiki/WiLAN "WiLAN") founders Hatim Zaghloul and Michel Fattouche invented [wideband](/wiki/Wideband "Wideband") [orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing](/wiki/Orthogonal_frequency-division_multiplexing "Orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing") (WOFDM), the basis for wideband [wireless communication](/wiki/Wireless_communication "Wireless communication") applications,[[55]](#cite_note-55) including [4G](/wiki/4G "4G") mobile communications.[[56]](#cite_note-ergen-56)

By 2009, it had become clear that, at some point, 3G networks would be overwhelmed by the growth of bandwidth-intensive applications, such as [streaming media](/wiki/Streaming_media "Streaming media").[[57]](#cite_note-57) Consequently, the industry began looking to data-optimized fourth-generation ([4G](/wiki/4G "4G")) technologies, with the promise of speed improvements up to ten-fold over existing 3G technologies. The first publicly available [LTE](/wiki/LTE_(telecommunication) "LTE (telecommunication)") service was launched in Scandinavia by [TeliaSonera](/wiki/TeliaSonera "TeliaSonera"), in 2009. In the 2010s, a 4G technology has found diverse applications across various sectors, showcasing its versatility in delivering high-speed wireless communication, such as mobile broadband, [internet of things](/wiki/Internet_of_things "Internet of things") (IoT), [fixed wireless access](/wiki/Fixed_wireless_access "Fixed wireless access"), and multimedia streaming (including music, video, [radio](/wiki/Internet_radio "Internet radio"), and [television](/wiki/Mobile_television "Mobile television")).

*How I Met Your Mother* was inspired by Carter Bays and Craig Thomas' idea to "write about our friends and the stupid stuff we did in New York", where they previously worked as writers for *[Late Show with David Letterman](/wiki/Late_Show_with_David_Letterman "Late Show with David Letterman")*, among others.[[1]](#cite_note-eonline-1) The two drew from their friendship in creating the characters. Ted is based loosely on Bays, and Marshall and Lily are based loosely on Thomas and his wife.[[5]](#cite_note-casting-5)[[6]](#cite_note-craig_thomas-6) Thomas' wife Rebecca was initially reluctant to have a character based on her but agreed if they could get [Alyson Hannigan](/wiki/Alyson_Hannigan "Alyson Hannigan") to play her. Hannigan was looking to do more comedy work and was available.[[5]](#cite_note-casting-5) [Josh Radnor](/wiki/Josh_Radnor "Josh Radnor") and [Jason Segel](/wiki/Jason_Segel "Jason Segel"), who were cast as Ted and Marshall, respectively, were not well known, although Segel had been a cast member on the short-lived *[Freaks and Geeks](/wiki/Freaks_and_Geeks "Freaks and Geeks")* and a recurring guest star on [Judd Apatow](/wiki/Judd_Apatow "Judd Apatow")'s follow-up show, *[Undeclared](/wiki/Undeclared "Undeclared")*. The **Western Front** was a [military theatre](/wiki/European_theatre_of_World_War_II "European theatre of World War II") of [World War II](/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") encompassing [Denmark](/wiki/Denmark "Denmark"), [Norway](/wiki/Norway "Norway"), [Luxembourg](/wiki/Luxembourg "Luxembourg"), [Belgium](/wiki/Belgium "Belgium"), the [Netherlands](/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands"), the [United Kingdom](/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom"), [France](/wiki/French_Third_Republic "French Third Republic"), and [Germany](/wiki/Nazi_Germany "Nazi Germany"). The [Italian front](/wiki/Italian_campaign_(World_War_II) "Italian campaign (World War II)") is considered a separate but related theatre.[[k]](#cite_note-49) The Western Front's 1944–1945 phase was officially deemed the [European Theater](/wiki/European_Theater_of_Operations,_United_States_Army "European Theater of Operations, United States Army") by the United States, whereas Italy fell under the [Mediterranean Theater](/wiki/Mediterranean_Theater_of_Operations,_United_States_Army "Mediterranean Theater of Operations, United States Army") along with the [North African campaign](/wiki/North_African_campaign "North African campaign"). The Western Front was marked by two phases of large-scale combat operations. The first phase saw the capitulation of Luxembourg, Netherlands, Belgium, and France during May and June 1940 after their defeat in the [Low Countries](/wiki/Low_Countries "Low Countries") and the northern half of France, and continued into an air war between Germany and Britain that climaxed with the [Battle of Britain](/wiki/Battle_of_Britain "Battle of Britain"). The second phase consisted of large-scale ground combat (supported by [a massive strategic air war](/wiki/Defence_of_the_Reich "Defence of the Reich") considered to be an additional front), which began in June 1944 with the [Allied landings in Normandy](/wiki/Normandy_landings "Normandy landi

On 20 February 1986, entrepreneur [Silvio Berlusconi](/wiki/Silvio_Berlusconi "Silvio Berlusconi") (who owned [Fininvest](/wiki/Fininvest "Fininvest") and [Mediaset](/wiki/Mediaset "Mediaset")) acquired the club and saved it from bankruptcy after investing vast amounts of money,[[11]](#cite_note-history-11) appointing rising manager [Arrigo Sacchi](/wiki/Arrigo_Sacchi "Arrigo Sacchi") at the helm of the *Rossoneri* and signing [Dutch](/wiki/Netherlands_national_football_team "Netherlands national football team") internationals [Ruud Gullit](/wiki/Ruud_Gullit "Ruud Gullit"), [Marco van Basten](/wiki/Marco_van_Basten "Marco van Basten") and [Frank Rijkaard](/wiki/Frank_Rijkaard "Frank Rijkaard").[[11]](#cite_note-history-11) The Dutch trio added an attacking impetus to the team, and complemented the club's [Italian](/wiki/Italy_national_football_team "Italy national football team") internationals [Paolo Maldini](/wiki/Paolo_Maldini "Paolo Maldini"), [Franco Baresi](/wiki/Franco_Baresi "Franco Baresi"), [Alessandro Costacurta](/wiki/Alessandro_Costacurta "Alessandro Costacurta") and [Roberto Donadoni](/wiki/Roberto_Donadoni "Roberto Donadoni"). Under Sacchi, Milan won its first Scudetto in nine years in the [1987–88 season](/wiki/1987%E2%80%9388_Serie_A "1987–88 Serie A"). The following year, the club won its first [European Cup](/wiki/1988%E2%80%9389_European_Cup "1988–89 European Cup") in two decades, beating Romanian club [Steaua București](/wiki/FC_Steaua_Bucure%C8%99ti "FC Steaua București") 4–0 in [the final](/wiki/1989_European_Cup_Final "1989 European Cup Final"). Further information: [History of the United Nations](/wiki/History_of_the_United_Nations "History of the United Nations")

In the century prior to the United Nation's creation, several international treaty organisations and conferences had been formed to regulate conflicts between nations, such as the [International Committee of the Red Cross](/wiki/International_Committee_of_the_Red_Cross "International Committee of the Red Cross") and the [Hague Conventions of 1899 and 1907](/wiki/Hague_Conventions_of_1899_and_1907 "Hague Conventions of 1899 and 1907").[[8]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKennedy20065-10) Following the catastrophic loss of life in [World War I](/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"), the [Paris Peace Conference](/wiki/Paris_Peace_Conference,_1919 "Paris Peace Conference, 1919") established the [League of Nations](/wiki/League_of_Nations "League of Nations") to maintain harmony between nations.[[9]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKennedy20068-11) The League successfully resolved some territorial disputes and created international structures for postal mail, aviation, and opium control, some of which were later absorbed into the UN.[[10]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKennedy200610-12) However, it lacked representation for colonial peoples – then half the world's population – and significant participation from several major powers, including the United States, the [USSR](/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union"), Germany, and Japan. It failed to act against the 1931 [Japanese invasion of Manchuria](/wiki/Japanese_invasion_of_Manchuria "Japanese invasion of Manchuria"), the [Second Italo-Ethiopian War](/wiki/Second_Italo-Ethiopian_War "Second Italo-Ethiopian War") in 1935, the 1937 [Japanese occupation of China](/wiki/Japanese_occupation_of_China "Japanese occupation of China"), and Nazi expansions under [Adolf Hitler](/wiki/Adolf_Hitler "Adolf Hitler") that escalated into World War II.[[11]](#cite_note-

The **Cairn of Barnenez** (also: **Barnenez Tumulus**, **Barnenez Mound**; in [Breton](/wiki/Breton_language "Breton language") *Karn Barnenez*; in [French](/wiki/French_language "French language"): *Cairn de Barnenez* or *Tumulus de Barnenez*) is a [Neolithic](/wiki/Neolithic "Neolithic") monument located near [Plouezoc'h](/wiki/Plouezoc%27h "Plouezoc'h"), on the Kernéléhen peninsula in northern [Finistère](/wiki/Finist%C3%A8re "Finistère"), [Brittany](/wiki/Brittany "Brittany"), [France](/wiki/France "France"). It dates to the early [Neolithic](/wiki/Neolithic "Neolithic"), around 4000 BC. Along with the [Tumulus of Bougon](/wiki/Tumulus_of_Bougon "Tumulus of Bougon") and [Locmariaquer megaliths](/wiki/Locmariaquer_megaliths "Locmariaquer megaliths"), also located in Great West France, it is one of the earliest [megalithic monuments](/wiki/Megaliths "Megaliths") in [Europe](/wiki/Europe "Europe") and one of the [oldest man-made structures in the world](/wiki/Oldest_buildings_in_the_world#By_age "Oldest buildings in the world").[[1]](#cite_note-1) It is also remarkable for the presence of [megalithic art](/wiki/Megalithic_art "

François Englert :: Academic career :: chunk_0001
He graduated as an electromechanical engineer in 1955 from the [Free University of Brussels](/wiki/Free_University_of_Brussels_(1834%E2%80%931969) "Free University of Brussels (1834–1969)") (ULB) where he received his PhD in physical sciences in 1959. From 1959 until 1961, he worked at [Cornell University](/wiki/Cornell_University "Cornell University"), first as a research associate of Robert Brout and then as assistant professor. He then returned to the ULB, where he became a university professor and was joined there by Robert Brout who, in 1980, with Englert coheaded the theoretical physics group. In 1998 Englert became professor emeritus. In 1984 Englert was first appointed as a Sackler Professor by Special Appointment in the School of Physics and Astronomy at [Tel-Aviv University](/wiki/Tel-Aviv_University "Tel-Aviv University"). Englert joined Chapman University's Institute for Quantum Studies in 2011, where he serves as a distinguished visiting professor.

QS World University Rankings :: Rankings :: QS World University Rankings: Regional Rankings :: chunk_0009
In addition to the World University Rankings, QS produces four regional rankings, including the Arab Region, Asia, Emerging Europe and Central Asia (discontinued), and Latin America. In 2023, QS launched the QS World University Rankings: Europe. These editions include an expanded roster of ranked universities for each region than those featured in the QS World University Rankings.

While the same methodological indicators tend to be used for the regional rankings, the weightings are modified and additional lenses are included to account for the unique characteristics of each region. Additional metrics include incoming and outgoing exchange students, academic staff with a PhD, and web visibility. Accordingly, the performance of institutions within their respective regional rankings can differ significantly from the QS World University Rankings released in the same academic year.[[27]](#cite_note-27)
